children: Our Bureau New Delhi: The government has, for the first time, invoked emergency provisions under Section 11 of the Electricity Act to direct captive coal-based power plants with more than 50 MW capacity to operate at their maximum available capacity in the next quarter to help meet electricity demand. Section 11 of the Electricity Act, 2003 allows the Centre, under extraordinary circumstances, to direct a power generation company to operate and maintain any generating station in accordance with its directions.

Captive coal-based power plants in India primarily supply electricity to aluminium, steel and cement units. The power ministry's September 25 directive covers more than 100 such generating units. The ministry's directive, published on its website, said that such electricity generators will offer surplus generation through the power exchanges. "The move will bring more liquidity in the power market and help states buy their requirements," a government official told ET. "These plants may use 51% for their consumption and sell the rest on the exchanges." Power consumption in India has grown by more than 14% so far in September, driven by cooling and irrigation demand amid a deficient monsoon.

Peak demand during the month has already topped the government's projection of 271 GW. The ministry's move comes amid expectations of higher electricity demand in the coming months. This month, prices in the Indian Energy Exchange's day-ahead market, particularly in the high-price segment and during non-solar hours, have touched the maximum of 20 a unit on several days.

title: Centre Asks Captive Coal Plants to Pull Max Output Lever
